title: The COVID-19 Infodemic: Twitter versus Facebook
screen_reason: Large-scale cross-platform analysis of links to low-credibility (MBFC-listed) domains in COVID-19 posts on Twitter and Facebook, 1 Jan - 31 Oct 2020. Yields (a) a CONTENT share of YouTube videos removed/made private, (b) CONCENTRATION pairs for verified accounts (small % of accounts, large % of reshares), and (c) the paper's headline low-to-high-credibility volume ratios. NOTE: the paper never reports a share of all COVID posts that are low-credibility - see notes.

estimates.platform: YouTube videos linked from Twitter and Facebook
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube videos shared in COVID-19 posts on both platforms that had been removed or made private (the paper's proxy for low-credibility video content)
estimates.value_raw: 1,828 (11%) of the 16,669 videos shared at least once on both platforms
estimates.denominator: 16,669 YouTube videos shared at least once on BOTH Twitter and Facebook among links in English COVID-19 keyword posts (out of over 64k videos linked on Twitter and 204k on Facebook)
estimates.definition: Video labelled suspicious if it had been removed by YouTube or made private at the time of the API query
estimates.misinfo_def: "we use removal of videos by YouTube as a proxy to label low-credibility content. We additionally consider private videos to be suspicious, since this can be used as a tactic to evade the platform's sanctions when violating terms of service."
estimates.source_quote: their metadata and focus on the 1,828 (11%) videos
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Label is YouTube's own removal / private status, not an author or fact-checker judgement. Validated by a two-step manual inspection of ~3% of unavailable videos (narratives recovered for 40 videos via bitchute.com and web copies), of which 90% contained misinformation. ground_truth coded 'classifier' as the closest available category for an automated platform-side label - none of the six options describes platform moderation exactly; an adjudicator may prefer 'researcher_coding'.
estimates.moderator_quote: We observed a high prevalence of links pointing to youtube.com on both platforms - over 64k videos on Twitter and 204k on Facebook. ... An approach analogous to the way we label links to websites would be to identify sources that upload low-credibility videos and then label every video from those sources as misinformation. However, this approach is infeasible because the list of YouTube channels would be huge and fluid. To circumvent this difficulty, we use removal of videos by YouTube as a proxy to label low-credibility content.
estimates.notes: Borderline because the numerator is a platform-moderation proxy (removed or private), not a veracity judgement; removal can happen for many reasons besides misinformation, and the authors' own validation on 40 videos suggests ~90% do carry misinformation. Denominator is the cross-platform intersection (videos shared on BOTH Twitter and Facebook), a non-random popularity-biased filter, hence denom_selection=curated. The authors state their estimates are lower bounds because deleted posts are absent from the collections. Quote trimmed to one line: this paper's two columns alternate line by line in the text rendering, so no sentence is contiguous. The passage reads: "To identify the most popular and suspicious YouTube content, we first select the 16,669 videos shared at least once on both platforms. We then query the YouTube API Videos:list endpoint to collect their metadata and focus on the 1,828 (11%) videos that had been removed or made private."

estimates.moderator_quote: We wish to measure whether low-credibility content originates from a wide range of users or can be attributed to a few influential actors. ... This suggests the existence of superspreaders: despite the diversity of root accounts publishing links to low-credibility content on both platforms, only messages from a small group of influential accounts are shared extensively.
estimates.notes: Satisfies R1 (both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct present). Flagged borderline for two reasons an adjudicator should weigh: (a) the group is defined by VERIFICATION STATUS, not by rank of activity, so it is not a 'top X% of users' in the usual concentration sense; (b) the share is read off Figure 8(c) and stated only as "almost 40%", so 40 is an upper-rounded approximation. Twitter data come from the Decahose (10% random sample of public tweets), biased toward active users. Quote trimmed to one line (columns alternate line by line). The passage reads: "Verified accounts are a small minority compared to unverified ones, that is, 1.9% on Twitter and 4.5% on Facebook, among root accounts involved in publishing low-credibility content. Despite this, Figure 8(c) shows that verified accounts yield almost 40% of low-credibility retweets on Twitter and almost 70% of reshares on Facebook." The line carrying the group size is "is, 1.9% on Twitter and 4.5% on Facebook, among".

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two-step manual inspection by the authors: deleted video IDs searched in other YouTube videos and web pages to recover titles, then titles searched on bitchute.com to find copies. No coder count, protocol or reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: we follow a two-step manual inspection process for a sample of about 3% of the unavailable videos, comprising a mix of randomly selected and popular ones
estimates.notes: R3 row: falsity computed INSIDE the suspicious (removed/private) video set, so within_misinfo_content=true - appendix only, never pooled with prevalence. It is the validity check for the 11% row: it says how often the removal proxy actually corresponds to misinformation. Sample is purposive (mix of random and popular) and small (n=40, and only those whose narrative could be recovered), so it is not an unbiased estimate of the positive predictive value. Source quote replaced (it was an ellipsis join) and trimmed to one line, ending on the line-break hyphen of "con-tain". The passage reads: "To validate this approach for identifying low-credibility YouTube content, we follow a two-step manual inspection process for a sample of about 3% of the unavailable videos, comprising a mix of randomly selected and popular ones. [...] This process allows us to identify the narratives of 40 deleted videos, 90% of which contain misinformation."

estimates.date: 1 February to 31 October 2020 (average of the daily series from February onward)
estimates.measure_type: RATIO of low-credibility to HIGH-credibility link volume on Twitter - NOT a share of all tweets
estimates.value_raw: "Twitter exhibits a higher ratio of low-credibility information than Facebook (32% vs. 21% on average)"
estimates.denominator: Volume of tweets+retweets linking to the 20 curated high-credibility domains (734,409 original tweets + 2,184,050 retweets = high-credibility volume, Table 3). The numerator is low-credibility volume (245,620 original tweets + 653,415 retweets).
estimates.definition: Daily volume of links to MBFC low-credibility domains divided by daily volume of links to the 20 curated high-credibility domains, averaged over the period from 1 February
estimates.misinfo_def: "We gather the sources labeled by MBFC as having a 'Very Low' or 'Low' factual-reporting level. We then add 'Questionable' or 'Conspiracy-Pseudoscience' sources"
estimates.source_quote: We finally observe that Twitter exhibits a higher ratio of low-credibility information than Facebook (32% vs. 21% on average).
estimates.page_loc: Results, "Prevalence trends", p. 6, with Figure 3(c) and Table 3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 674 MBFC low-credibility domains as numerator; benchmark denominator is a hand-curated list of 20 high-credibility outlets spanning the US political spectrum (MBFC 'Mixed' or higher) plus cdc.gov and who.int.
estimates.moderator_quote: (c) Daily ratio of volume of low-credibility links to volume of high-credibility links on Twitter and Facebook. ... The horizontal lines indicate averages across the period starting February 1.
estimates.notes: CRITICAL CODING WARNING - this is the number most likely to be mis-extracted from this paper. 32% is NOT the share of COVID tweets that are low-credibility; it is the ratio of low-credibility to HIGH-credibility link volume (Figure 3c). Table 3 confirms it: 899,035 low-credibility / 2,918,459 high-credibility = 30.8%, close to the stated 32%. Coded construct OTHER (hence denom_scope n/a) precisely so it cannot be pooled as a prevalence. A share of low among low+high would be 23.6%, but that is a cross-category sum R8 forbids, and it is still not a share of all COVID content. The paper never reports a share of all posts/tweets that are low-credibility.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) NO true prevalence (share of ALL COVID posts that are low-credibility) is reported anywhere in the paper. Table 3 gives absolute counts by credibility class only, and the collection totals ("over 53M tweets", "over 37M posts") are approximate and not on the same basis as the reshare/retweet counts, so no share of all content can be derived without a forbidden computation. (2) Domain-level concentration examples not entered as rows because they are illustrative single-domain statistics: on Twitter "about 20% of the retweets containing links to thegatewaypundit.com pertain to @gatewaypundit ... The remaining retweets have 10,410 different root users" (1 of 10,411 roots -> 20% of retweets); on Facebook "among all 2,821 pages/groups that post links to thegatewaypundit.com, the official page @gatewaypundit accounts for 68% of the reshares" (1 of 2,821 pages -> 68% of reshares). Both formally satisfy R1 and could be added as source-level CONCENTRATION rows if the review wants per-domain concentration. (3) "we extract the top user/page/group ... for each source and find that 19% and 21% of them are verified on Twitter and Facebook" and "most of the top low-credibility sources have official accounts on both Twitter and Facebook, which tend to be verified (71.4% on Twitter and 65.2% on Facebook). They are also the top spreaders of those domains in 16 of 21 cases (76.2%) on Twitter and 18 of 23 (78.3%) on Facebook" - these describe who the top spreaders are, not a share of exposure or sharing, so they are not R1 concentration pairs. (4) "a power law nh ~ nb^c with exponent c ~ 1.04, suggesting a weak level of bot amplification (4%)" is an amplification exponent, not a share with a denominator. (5) Figure 7 (percentage of suspicious videos by percent rank) is reported only graphically. (6) Survey statistics quoted from Pew (69% of US adults use Facebook, 22% Twitter, 43% / 12% news pathway) are cited from elsewhere and are about platform use, not misinformation - excluded by R8. (7) The 2.7:1 retweet-to-tweet and 68:1 reshare-to-post ratios are volume ratios, not prevalence.

rob.design: Cross-platform observational study, 1 January - 31 October 2020. Twitter: English tweets containing 'coronavirus', 'COVID', 'sars' from the Decahose (10% random sample of public tweets) via the Observatory on Social Media API - over 53M tweets from about 12M users; sampling is per-tweet so the user sample is biased toward active users. Facebook: same keywords, English posts by public pages and groups via the CrowdTangle posts/search endpoint - over 37M posts from over 140k pages/groups; CrowdTangle covers pages/groups above follower thresholds plus researcher-requested additions, which the authors warn may over-represent low-credibility pages. Misinformation labelled at SOURCE level by matching (and expanding 49 URL-shortener services) against 674 MBFC low-credibility domains (Very Low/Low factual reporting, Questionable, Conspiracy-Pseudoscience); benchmark of 20 hand-picked high-credibility outlets plus CDC and WHO. YouTube videos labelled suspicious by removal/private status, validated on 40 recovered narratives (90% misinformation). Concentration measured with inverse normalized entropy; coordination via TF-IDF co-domain networks with similarity thresholds (0.99 Twitter, 0.95 Facebook) chosen by manual inspection; bots via BotometerLite at threshold 0.5 (Twitter only). No human content coding, so no inter-coder reliability. IRB-exempt. Authors state estimates are LOWER BOUNDS because deleted content is absent, note source-level labelling is 'necessary but not ideal', and that the low-credibility list was not tailored to COVID-19.
rob.item6_quote: We define our list of low-credibility domains based on information provided by the Media Bias/Fact Check website (MBFC, mediabiasfactcheck.com), an independent organization that reviews and rates the reliability of news sources. We gather the sources labeled by MBFC as having a "Very Low" or "Low" factual-reporting level. We then add "Questionable" or "Conspiracy-Pseudoscience" sources and we leave out those with factual-reporting levels of "Mostly-Factual," "High," or "Very High."
rob.item10_quote: To identify the most popular and suspicious YouTube content, we first select the 16,669 videos shared at least once on both platforms. We then query the YouTube API Videos:list endpoint to collect their metadata and focus on the 1,828 (11%) videos that had been removed or made private.
